items.prompt: Two updates use the same three true facts but lead with different ones. What is that?
choices: Lying, because the two updates disagree with each other
Framing, because only order and emphasis changed
Spin, because one update sounds happier than the other
items.explanation: Both updates keep all three facts, so the difference is in order and emphasis only.

items.prompt: Which of these is spin?
choices: Leaving out the outage while every sentence stays true
Putting the 40.6% speed-up in the first sentence
Writing that the outage lasted an hour when it lasted 12 minutes
items.explanation: Spin drops a material fact. Leading with the win is framing, and misstating the duration is lying.

items.prompt: Which of these is lying?
choices: Mentioning the outage in the last paragraph of the update
Leading with the speed-up before mentioning the delay
Writing that the project had no outage when it did
items.explanation: A lie states something false. The other two only change where true facts sit.

items.prompt: Does framing require changing any fact?
choices: Yes, one fact must be softened to fit the story
Yes, the weakest fact must be dropped from the update
No, the facts stay identical; only emphasis moves
items.explanation: Framing leaves the facts untouched. If a fact changes or disappears, it is no longer framing.

items.prompt: In the L1 scenario, what was the measurable win?
choices: Page loads got 40.6% faster
The project shipped three weeks early
There were no outages at all
items.explanation: Page load time went from 3.2s to 1.9s, which is 40.6% faster.

items.prompt: In the L1 scenario, what was the miss?
choices: The project shipped three days late
The project shipped three weeks late
The project shipped three months late
items.explanation: A 6-week estimate became 9 weeks, so the miss was three weeks.

items.prompt: What is emphasis?
choices: How much room or lead position a fact gets
Whether a fact is good news or bad news
Whether a fact is checked against its original source
items.explanation: Emphasis is the dial framing turns: space and position, independent of whether the fact is positive.

items.prompt: Saying 'I got a high grade' while hiding that your partner did all the work is which of these?
choices: Framing, since the grade is allowed to lead the story
Lying, since the grade was made up by the author
Spin, since no sentence is false but the overall picture is
items.explanation: The grade is real, so it is not a lie, but the work split changes how the result is judged, so dropping it is spin.

items.prompt: An update claims 'this was a one-off outage' when the same bug caused two earlier outages. Everything else is accurate. What is the best classification?
choices: Spin, since an earlier outage is missing from the update
Framing, since the author chose how to characterize it
Lying, since it asserts something false about the past
Neither, since 'one-off' is only the author's opinion of it
items.explanation: 'One-off' is a factual claim that the history contradicts, so a stated fact is false. That makes it lying, not omission.
items.reference:
Three things you can do with the same facts
🔀 Framing: order and emphasis change
🕳️ Spin: a material fact is missing
✖️ Lying: a stated fact is false
Why: each one breaks a different thing, so each needs its own check.
items.learnMore:
Framing, spin and lying are three different acts

Framing rearranges true facts. Spin keeps every sentence true but drops something the reader needed. Lying states something false. Only the first is legitimate.

Common mistake

Treating spin as acceptable because no single sentence is false.
items.reflection: Think of a story you were once told where every sentence was true but you later felt misled. Which fact was missing?

items.prompt: An author keeps all three facts, leads with the speed-up, and gives the 12-minute outage a plain sentence at the end. Which verdict fits?
choices: Framing: nothing is false and nothing is missing
Spin, since the outage does not get first position
Lying, since the order implies the outage was minor
Spin, since the speed-up sits ahead of the delay
items.explanation: Both checks pass, and position alone is not an omission. Emphasis is the author's to choose.

items.prompt: What is narrative ownership?
choices: Deciding which facts to hide from your colleagues
Telling the story of your own work yourself, early
Letting colleagues tell the story of your work for you
items.explanation: Owning the narrative means proactively telling it instead of leaving it to be assembled secondhand.

items.prompt: If you say nothing about your project, what happens to its story?
choices: It stays untold until someone asks you about it
Others assemble it from whatever they heard first
It stays neutral because nobody forms any view of it
items.explanation: People form a view regardless. Silence just hands the framing to someone else.

items.prompt: Is reporting events in the order they happened a neutral choice?
choices: Yes, order never affects how a story reads
Yes, since no facts have been changed
No, it is one frame chosen by default
items.explanation: Order decides what a reader meets first, so it is a frame like any other.

items.prompt: What fills the gap when you do not frame your own work?
choices: The reader's own assumptions
A neutral summary of the facts
The facts speaking for themselves
items.explanation: With no deliberate frame, readers fill the gap with assumptions or first impressions.

items.prompt: When is the best time to tell the story of a project with a setback?
choices: Only after someone asks about it in a meeting
Early, before a secondhand version forms
After the setback has been forgotten by everyone
items.explanation: An early, honest telling gets there before rumor or first impressions do.

items.prompt: Telling your own story honestly means which of these?
choices: Choosing order and emphasis while keeping every material fact
Deciding which facts count as true for the reader
Keeping the bad news back until someone asks about it
items.explanation: You control order and emphasis. You never control what is true or which material facts appear.

items.prompt: What does silence about a setback usually do?
choices: Makes the setback quietly disappear from people's minds
Keeps the story neutral for everyone who hears it
Lets someone else's first version become the story
items.explanation: The setback is still known; only your voice is missing from how it is told.

items.prompt: Which of these is part of owning the story?
choices: Waiting for a reviewer to find the miss
Describing the miss only as 'some issues'
Naming the miss yourself, with its cause and its size
items.explanation: Naming the miss and its cause yourself is what makes the account yours and credible.

items.prompt: Your project had a win and a miss. You post nothing, and a teammate describes it in a corridor, starting with the miss. What best describes what happened?
choices: No framing happened, because nothing was published
The teammate lied by starting with the miss
The story stayed neutral because you added nothing
The framing went to whoever spoke first
items.explanation: Someone always frames the story. By staying silent you gave up the choice of what leads.
items.reference:
Who tells the story of your work
🗣️ You, early: you pick order and emphasis
💬 Someone else: their first impression leads
🤐 Silence: the gap gets filled anyway
Why: the story is told either way, so the only choice is who frames it.
items.learnMore:
Silence is not neutral

If you do not explain your work, someone assembles the story from the first fact they heard. Owning the narrative means telling it yourself, honestly, with the material facts included.

Common mistake

Believing that saying nothing keeps the story free of framing.

items.prompt: Two people give honest accounts of the same quarter. One reports month by month, the other leads with the result. Which statement is correct?

Both frame; one by choice, one by habit
Only the month-by-month report is honest
Neither frames anything, since both are accurate
items.explanation: Chronological order is also a frame. The difference is deliberateness, not honesty.

Announcing the win and answering delay questions only if asked
Waiting until the delay is discovered, then explaining it
Mentioning the delay only to the one manager who asks

Letting people decide is itself a form of spin
Choosing what goes first and last is already a framing decision

items.explanation: Any selection and ordering of facts is a frame, even when it is made without thought.

items.prompt: What is a material fact?
choices: A fact that would change a fair reader's judgment
Any fact that happens to be true about the project work
A fact the author personally thinks is important
items.explanation: Materiality is about the reader's judgment, not the author's view or mere truth.

items.prompt: Does an honest update have to include every detail?
choices: Yes, every single detail
No, only the material ones
Only the details that sound positive
items.explanation: Honesty needs the material facts. Trivia can be skipped.

items.prompt: Is 'the team used one editor over another' usually material to a rollout's outcome?
choices: No, it changes nobody's judgment of the result
Yes, every tooling choice is material to the outcome
Yes, if the decision was made recently enough
items.explanation: It has no bearing on how the rollout went, so omitting it is fine.

items.prompt: Is 'a 12-minute outage' material to how a rollout went?
choices: No, it was over quickly and has already been fixed
No, it only matters to the people on the on-call team
Yes, it changes how risky the rollout looks
items.explanation: A reader judging the rollout would change their view on learning about the outage.

items.prompt: Who is the 'reasonable reader'?
choices: Someone looking for reasons to criticize the author
A normal person who is trying to judge the result fairly
Someone who accepts whatever is written
items.explanation: Materiality is judged by a fair reader, neither hostile nor easily satisfied.

items.prompt: Is 'my partner did all the work' material to whether you earned the group grade?
choices: No, only the final grade itself matters to anyone
Yes, it changes who deserves the credit
No, since the grade is already high
items.explanation: It bears directly on the thing being judged, so it is material.

items.prompt: Is the poster font material to how much money an event raised?
choices: Yes, design always decides donations
Yes, any visible detail is material
No, it has no bearing on the amount raised
items.explanation: The font does not change the amount raised, so leaving it out is harmless.

items.prompt: Materiality depends mainly on which of these?
choices: What the reader is trying to judge
How long the fact takes to explain
How embarrassing the fact is
items.explanation: The same fact can be material for one judgment and irrelevant for another.

items.prompt: An update omits that the main test suite was switched off for the last two weeks. Readers are judging whether the release is safe. Is the omission material?
choices: No, test setup is an internal detail
Yes, it changes how safe the release looks to a reader
No, the release shipped successfully anyway
Only if a bug appears later
items.explanation: Reasonable readers judging safety would revise their view, so it is material whatever happens afterward.
items.reference:
Material or not, for the same update
🐛 12-minute outage: material
✏️ Which editor the team used: not material
👥 Partner did all the work: material
Why: a fact is material when a reasonable reader's judgment would change.
items.learnMore:
Materiality, not completeness, is the test

An honest update need not list every detail. It must include every fact that would change a reasonable reader's understanding of the outcome.

Common mistake

Thinking honesty means including everything, or that it can ignore anything that is inconvenient.

items.prompt: How many questions are in the honesty check?
choices: One
Two
Three
items.explanation: One about truth and one about material facts.

items.prompt: What does question 1 ask?
choices: Is every stated fact in the update true?
Is every sentence upbeat?
Is the order chronological?
items.explanation: Question 1 checks the truth of what is stated, which catches lying.

items.prompt: What does question 2 ask?
choices: Is every detail from the project included?
Is every fact in the update positive?
Is every material fact included?
items.explanation: Question 2 is about material facts only, which catches spin.

items.prompt: A draft that fails question 1 is which of these?
choices: Spin
Framing
Lying
items.explanation: A false stated fact is a lie, whatever else the draft does.

items.prompt: A draft that passes question 1 but fails question 2 is which of these?
choices: Spin
Lying
Framing
items.explanation: Every sentence is true, yet a material fact is missing: that is spin.

items.prompt: A draft that passes both questions is which of these?
choices: Spin with true wording
Honest framing
A lie told gently
items.explanation: Both checks pass, so order and emphasis are the author's choice.

items.prompt: When should you run the check?
choices: Before the update is sent to anyone
After someone questions it
Only for long updates
items.explanation: It is meant to be run before sending, not assembled later as a defense.

items.prompt: Does passing both questions prove the update is well told?
choices: Yes, it also proves the update is well told
Yes, provided the update stays short enough
No, it proves honesty, not quality
items.explanation: A draft can be honest and still poorly ordered, like Draft A in L3.

items.prompt: A draft is entirely true, omits a material fact, and leads with the win. Where does the check stop it?
choices: At question 1, since leading with the win seems selective
Nowhere, because leading with a win is allowed
At question 2, which finds the missing material fact
At question 1, since an omission counts as untrue
items.explanation: Leading with the win is fine, but question 2 fails on the missing fact.
items.reference:
The two-question check
1️⃣ Is every stated fact true? No means lying
2️⃣ Is every material fact present? No means spin
✅ Both yes: honest framing
Why: each question catches a different failure, so neither can stand in for the other.
items.learnMore:
Two independent questions

Question 1 catches lying; question 2 catches spin. Passing both proves honesty, not good writing. Run them before sending, not as a defense afterward.

Common mistake

Replacing the two questions with a vague feeling that the draft seems honest.
items.reflection: Run the two questions on the last status update you wrote. Which one did you rely on more without noticing?

items.prompt: Why keep the two questions separate instead of asking 'does this feel honest'?
choices: Each catches a different failure; neither replaces the other
The first catches all dishonesty, so the second is merely optional
Combining them would make the check slower to run
The second only matters for updates longer than a page
items.explanation: Lying and spin are different failures. A draft can clear one and fail the other.

choices: No, it has no framing at all
Yes, a default one
No, it is automatically neutral
items.explanation: Order always decides what the reader meets first, so it is a frame.

items.prompt: 'First we failed, then we fixed it' and 'we delivered, after a failure we fixed' can both be honest if they do what?
choices: Use the same sentence order
Include the same material facts
Contain the same number of sentences
items.explanation: Honesty depends on facts, not on sentence order.

items.prompt: What does first position in an update carry?
choices: The least weight with the reader
No particular weight at all
The most weight in the reader's impression
items.explanation: Readers weight what they meet first most heavily.

items.prompt: If you choose no frame, who chooses it?
choices: Habit, or whoever tells it next
The facts, which frame themselves in order
Nobody does, since no frame exists
items.explanation: The frame still exists; it is just not yours.

items.prompt: Which approach avoids framing entirely?
choices: Strict chronological order, since it adds nothing
None, since any order is a frame
Listing only the positive facts
items.explanation: Every ordering of facts is a choice of some kind.

items.prompt: What is the real alternative to careless framing?
choices: Choosing order and emphasis on purpose
Refusing to put the facts in any order
Removing all emphasis from the update
items.explanation: You cannot avoid ordering, so you choose it deliberately.

items.prompt: Calling chronological order 'neutral' mainly hides what?
choices: That the facts were changed
That the update is true
That a choice was made
items.explanation: The label hides that a decision, even a default one, occurred.

items.prompt: Compare 'failure then fix' with 'delivery then failure.' Are the facts the same?
choices: No, the second adds new facts
No, the first drops the fix
Yes, only the order of the facts differs
items.explanation: Same material facts, so only the frame differs.

items.prompt: Update A reports a rollout month by month, outage in month 3 of 4. Update B leads with the result and mentions the outage second. Both include the same material facts. Which is true?
choices: Only B is framing, because A did not choose its order
Only A is honest, because it keeps the original sequence
B is spin, because it moves the outage away from the lead
Both are honest frames; they differ in what the reader sees first
items.explanation: Both pass both checks. They differ in emphasis, not in honesty.

Why: whatever comes first carries the most weight, chosen or not.

items.prompt: A quarter had a success in week 2 and a failure in week 11. A strict timeline ends on the failure. What is the likely effect on the reader's overall impression?
choices: The ending leaves extra weight on the failure
None, since the reader weighs both facts equally
The success is forgotten because it came first
The reader will treat the report as dishonest
items.explanation: What ends the account tends to linger, so a default order can tilt the impression without any decision.
items.reference:
Two honest orders, same facts
📅 Failed first, then fixed: ends on the fix
🏁 Delivered, after a failure we fixed: ends on the result
⚖️ Same material facts, different first impression
Why: whatever comes first carries the most weight, chosen or not.
items.learnMore:
Chronological order is a frame too

Reporting in the order things happened feels neutral, but it is just a default frame. The honest alternative is choosing order and emphasis on purpose, with both checks still passing.

Common mistake

Believing that skipping the decision means no decision was made.
items.reflection: Think of a report you gave in strict time order. What would have changed if you had led with the outcome?

items.prompt: Which edit changes the frame without changing honesty?
choices: Replacing 'outage' with 'brief hiccup' in the delay sentence
Dropping the delay to keep the update short
Moving the result ahead of the delay, keeping both facts
Mentioning the delay only to people who ask about it
items.explanation: Moving facts around keeps both checks passing. The other edits soften, drop or hide facts.

items.prompt: Does Draft A (the buried-lead version) pass the honesty check?
choices: Yes, nothing is false and nothing material is missing
No, it hides the outage from readers behind vague wording
No, it contains a false claim about the delay
items.explanation: Draft A names the outage and the delay, so it passes both questions.

items.prompt: Which draft leaves the outage out entirely?
choices: Draft A
Draft C
Draft B
items.explanation: Draft C never mentions the outage.

items.prompt: What is Draft C an example of?
choices: Spin: every sentence is true, but a material fact is missing
Lying, since it states untrue things about the outage
Framing, since the order of the facts is chosen
items.explanation: Draft C leaves out a material fact without stating anything false.

items.prompt: Which draft gives the outage both a cause and a fix?
choices: Draft A
Draft C
Draft B
items.explanation: Draft B names the cause, the 12-minute duration and the regression test.

items.prompt: What is Draft A's main weakness?
choices: It contains a false statement about the delay
The win is buried behind the setback
It leaves out the delay entirely
items.explanation: Draft A is honest, but the 40.6% win is reduced to a vague clause at the end.

items.prompt: Which two drafts are both honest?
choices: B and C
A and B
A and C
items.explanation: A and B pass both questions; C fails the second.

items.prompt: What does a reader of Draft B know that a reader of Draft C does not?
choices: That page loads got faster after the change
That the caching logic was part of the work
That an outage happened during the rollout itself
items.explanation: Draft C is silent about the outage, which is the key difference.

items.prompt: What does Draft B lead with?
choices: The measured 40.6% speed-up
An apology for the delay and the outage
The cause of the outage and its fix
items.explanation: B opens with the result, giving real numbers, then covers the delay and outage.

items.prompt: Which single change would turn Draft C into honest framing with the fewest edits?
choices: Replace 'a bit longer' with 'a little longer'
Add the 12-minute outage and note it was fixed
Move the 40.6% figure to the end of the update
Delete the sentence about added complexity in the caching
items.explanation: Draft C fails only because the outage is missing. Adding it fixes question 2 without touching the rest.
items.reference:
Scoring the three drafts
😔 A: all facts, setback leads: honest
✅ B: all facts, win leads: honest
🚩 C: outage missing: spin
Why: only C fails question 2, and it fails by what it leaves out.
items.learnMore:
Same facts, three verdicts

Draft A and B both pass the check; B is simply better ordered and more specific. Draft C is the only one that crosses the line, by omitting the outage entirely.

Common mistake

Calling Draft A more honest because it opens with the bad news.

B chose its emphasis and named specifics for every reader

choices: Twelve hours
Twelve minutes
Twelve seconds

items.prompt: What does 'proportion' ask about a fact?
choices: Whether it gets room matching its weight
Whether it comes first in the update, before any others
Whether it is good news or bad news
items.explanation: Proportion compares the space a fact gets with how serious it is.

items.prompt: As an outage gets more serious, a one-clause mention does what?
choices: Fits it better
Fits it exactly as well
Fits it less well
items.explanation: A heavier fact needs more room than a short clause provides.

items.prompt: Which is a sign a serious fact is under-explained?
choices: It is named with its cause, its size and its fix
It includes a step that prevents a repeat
It is just called 'brief' or 'some issues'
items.explanation: Vague wording lets the reader miss the size of the problem.

items.prompt: Can a brief mention of a very serious fact still mislead?
choices: Yes, even when every sentence in it is true
No, any mention at all counts as honest
No, provided the mention is accurate
items.explanation: Proportion can fail even when both questions pass.

items.prompt: What should the account of a heavier outage add?
choices: A more cheerful opening paragraph for readers
Who was affected and how it is prevented
Fewer details so nobody is alarmed
items.explanation: Impact and prevention are what a heavier fact needs.

items.prompt: In the interactive demo, what grows as the outage gets longer while the text stays the same?
choices: How much the brief mention reads as spin
The size of the speed-up in the update
The length of the update overall as it is edited
items.explanation: The gap between room given and room deserved widens.

items.prompt: How does L3 describe the three-drafts example?
choices: A rule that covers every kind of update
A template to copy word for word into updates
One worked case, not the whole territory
items.explanation: Different audiences and stakes change what an honest update needs.

items.prompt: The outage grows from 12 minutes to 4 hours and hits paying customers. Which response is most honest?
choices: Move the outage to the top and drop the win to avoid bias
Keep Draft B's wording, since every sentence is still true
Keep the win first, but give the outage real room
Remove the speed-up so the outage is not overshadowed
items.explanation: Order may stay, but the outage needs room matching its weight.
items.reference:
Room matched to weight
⏱️ 12-minute outage: a clause and a fix fits
🧑‍🤝‍🧑 4-hour outage with paying customers: needs real space
📏 Same sentences, heavier fact: reads as spin
Why: a brief mention of a heavy fact can mislead like an omission, even though nothing is false.
items.learnMore:
Proportion is the gradient beside the bright line

Omission and false statements are the bright line. Beside it, the heavier a fact is, the more room it needs before a brief mention starts working like an omission.

Common mistake

Reusing the same short treatment for a much bigger incident.
items.reflection: Think of a bad piece of news you once softened. Did its weight match the room it got?
